Riemann sums are approximations to the area under a curve, formed by partitioning the interval from a to b into subintervals, constructing rectangles over each subinterval, and summing their areas. As the partition width shrinks and the number of rectangles increases, the Riemann sum converges to the Riemann integral, making Riemann sums the formal definition of what we mean by "the signed area under a curve."

To set up a Riemann sum, you partition the interval from a to b into n subintervals, each of width delta x equals b minus a divided by n. Over each subinterval from x of i minus one to x of i, you choose a sample point c sub i. The Riemann sum is then the sum from i equals one to n of f of c sub i times delta x.

You can construct different types of Riemann sums depending on your choice of sample points. The left sum uses the left endpoint of each subinterval. The right sum uses the right endpoint. The midpoint sum uses the midpoint of each subinterval. The trapezoidal rule averages left and right sums and approximates the curve with trapezoids instead of rectangles.

As n approaches infinity, delta x approaches zero, and the Riemann sum converges to the definite integral of f from a to b for continuous or Riemann-integrable functions. This limit defines the definite integral—no antiderivatives needed, just the area computation. Remarkably, different choices of sample points—left, right, or midpoint—all converge to the same integral for continuous functions.

Riemann sums bridge intuition and formality. They are the computational foundation of integration. Conceptually, they capture the intuitive idea of stacking rectangles to approximate area, while the limit provides formal precision. In practice, Riemann sums and their cousins like the trapezoidal rule and Simpson's rule are how numerical integration is implemented: computers cannot compute antiderivatives symbolically, so they approximate via Riemann sums. The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus tells us that computing the limit of Riemann sums is equivalent to evaluating F of b minus F of a—a profound insight connecting area, antiderivatives, and accumulation. Quiz-bowl questions test understanding of how Riemann sums approximate integrals, recognizing whether particular sums give overestimates or underestimates, and computing them explicitly for simple functions.
